description: Our team for NASA Apps challenge 2026 at Haifa.
summary:
Our Solution: " Unseen Earth"
Floods are mapped from space every day, but today’s main services, such as the Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM), mostly use C-band radar (Sentinel-1). That radar sees open water well but misses water hidden under trees and tall plants. Large flooded forests and wetlands, like the Amazon várzea, the Congo swamps, the Okavango and the Inner Niger Delta, end up missing from the map. We use NASA’s new NISAR satellite, whose longer L-band radar passes through the vegetation, to find this hidden flood water and add it where the current picture has gaps. We then combine it with Canadian Space Agency radar. RADARSAT-1 archives going back to the 1990s let us compare then with now, and the RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) gives an independent check of the same floods. This shows what each sensor is good at: NISAR sees under the canopy, and RCM revisits often in fine detail. Everything is shown on one interactive map, so anyone can see where the water really is, how it has changed over the years, and why NISAR adds to what existing flood services show.
We aim to partner with Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) so they can add our hidden-flood layer to their service, and to offer it to global insurers who need the full extent of flood damage.
details:
Unseen Earth fills in the blank areas of today’s flood maps. The flood map responders rely on most, Copernicus GFM, uses Sentinel-1’s 5.6 cm C-band radar. That signal can’t get through dense vegetation or built-up areas, so GFM marks flooded forest and towns “cannot see”. NASA-ISRO’s NISAR uses a 24 cm L-band wave, which passes through the leaves. Open water shows up dark. Flooded forest shows up bright, because the water and the tree trunks bounce the signal back like a corner reflector. Our open-source Python pipeline takes NISAR GCOV backscatter (HH + HV, 80 m, every 12 days) for each flood site and stacks the passes on one track. It then detects water with a per-scene threshold (Martinis et al. 2015) plus L-band features: change from the dry season, HV, and 12-day GUNW coherence. It finds water under trees with the double-bounce rule from the NISAR Science Users’ Handbook and removes permanent water. Finally, it counts only the water inside GFM’s “cannot see” mask. The result is the official map plus what NISAR adds. On a web map you can follow each flood over time, swipe between then and now, and look back decades with CSA’s RADARSAT-1 archive.

Benefits and impact: Across 16 flood sites in 2026, NISAR found 873 km² of flood water where the official maps can’t see. At the median site that’s +47% more flooded area. These are the areas where people live under the canopy (Amazon várzea, Tonle Sap, the Congo, the Mekong) and where relief can miss them. We didn’t build a competing product: we wrote a guide for adding L-band to GFM’s mask. We checked our results only against data we didn’t detect with:

  • 88% pixel agreement with Canada’s RCM radar within 3 days at the Peace–Athabasca Delta
  • mean F1 0.69–0.79 against NASA OPERA DSWx-HLS on clear days
  • precision 0.95–1.00 against USGS EDEN water gauges in the Everglades

We present every area as a lower bound, and the limits are stated openly on our Science page.

Tools and creativity: Python (numpy, scipy, h5py, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, asf_search) for the offline pipeline. A static HTML/JS site with Leaflet, hosted on Vercel. Data from NASA Earthdata/ASF (NISAR GCOV and GUNW, OPERA DSWx, HLS, GIBS), Copernicus GFM, ESA WorldCover, CSA RCM and RADARSAT-1, and USGS EDEN. Claude Code helped as a coding and writing assistant. The creative idea is to complement the existing map rather than replace it: we measure exactly what it misses, show it in place on the map, and link a 2026 radar to 30 years of Canadian radar history. We also weighed scientific honesty (independent checks, provisional NISAR calibration, a sample of chosen sites rather than global totals) and a focused, demoable app that keeps the user on one map.
